The crate sat high on Wren's back, lashed to the frame at four corners, and in eleven miles it had not moved a finger's width. That was the trouble with a good load. A bad one announced itself. A good one only put on weight.

The Ferrous Gate arrived out of the haze the way it always arrived, all at once: two iron posts driven into the roadbed, a lintel laid across them, and above that nothing at all. No wall. No fence. Nothing between a man and the open country on either side. Men had gone around. The Road entered that as a debt as well, and set a harder price on it.

Wren halted at the white line, eight paces short, and lowered the frame's foot onto the stone. His shoulders held the shape of the straps a while longer.

The toll board hung from the left post, and the System kept it honest:

**FERROUS GATE — POSTED TOLL**
**Passage, laden: 7 days**
**Sealed cargo: subject to inspection**

Seven. He had walked the whole stretch with seven in mind. He pushed his thumb under the strap where it had bitten, and kept his eyes on the figures, since now and then they changed while a man looked at them.

The collector's window was a slot cut in the right post at elbow height, and Haro's ledger came through it ahead of Haro: a wide splayed book with a spine like a wagon axle, opened flat on the sill. Then the man himself. Long grey coat, a ring of gate-keys he was never seen to use, and the face of someone who had spent years going down columns.

"Name."

"You know my name."

"The book doesn't." Haro's eyes stayed on the page. "Name."

"Idren." He gave it the way he always gave it, a word borrowed out of some other tongue. "Wren, on the road."

The pen found his line. **IDREN — porter, indentured, Ferrous Gate.** Under it ran a column of small dates going back a year and change, a number set against each, and at the bottom the two figures Wren could find without reading a thing above them.

**Days owed: 4,027**
**Days paid: 52**

"Laden," Haro said. "Sealed?"

"Sealed."

"Set it down."

Wren backed the frame to the post and freed the ropes, and the crate lifted off his spine with that terrible lightness that never once resembled relief. Pale banded wood, and across the lid a wax seal the colour of a burn gone over to scar, stamped with a mark he did not recognize and had never asked after. He had carried it since the low bridges. It did not slosh. It did not knock. Whatever lay inside it lay there exactly.

Haro let himself out by the gate's small door, walked once around the crate, and laid two fingers on the seal without breaking it. He held still that way for a moment, in the manner of a physician.

"Seven for the passage," he said. "Two for the seal. Gate's discretion on unopened cargo."

"The board says seven."

"The board says *sealed cargo: subject to inspection.* This is the inspection." He lifted his fingers off the wax. "Nine days."

Wren worked the arithmetic he had worked a thousand times and would work a thousand more, and it came out the way it always came out, which was no. Nine was nine. Nine was a fortnight of some winter forty years off, an afternoon he would now never be given, spent instead on this cold stone, arguing about wax.

"Nine," he said.

"Consent aloud. You know the form."

"I consent to the toll of nine days against passage of the Ferrous Gate, laden and sealed."

The System took them.

It was not pain. He had said so to a man once, and the man had not believed him, and after that Wren had given up the explaining. It was subtraction. Something down in the meat of him that had been keeping count since the hour he was born stepped back nine, and his knees understood before the rest of him did, and the cold came up out of the stone through his boots and met less resistance than it had a minute before. He let his breath go. Past the gate, the haze stood exactly as it had stood.

**TOLL PAID — 9 days**
**FERROUS GATE — passage granted, laden, sealed**

Haro was already writing. The pen crossed the ledger in three strokes, and Wren watched the two figures at the foot of his column go under the line and rise again below it.

**Days owed: 4,018**
**Days paid: 61**

Then the receipt: a chit of grey card with the day's mark pressed into it still wet, slid over the sill under one finger.

Wren took it. He drew his own book out of his coat, a cheap sewn thing whose first four pages had swollen in a river, and set down the date and *Ferrous, laden+seal, 9* and the running total beneath it in his own hand, because a man who keeps no count of his own is only holding somebody else's.

He was forming the 61 when his eye went up the page.

Above his line stood the last porter's: a woman's name that meant nothing to him, four entries, and at the foot of them a paid-total that did not agree with what those four entries made. Not by much. By one.

"Something," Haro said.

"No." Wren blew across the ink. "Nothing."

He got the frame onto his shoulders and took the crate's weight back onto a spine nine days shorter, and walked under the lintel, and the iron let him by without touching him.

A load tied badly kept telling you where it was, knocking at the shoulder blade, tugging left on the corners, so at least you knew the shape of what you carried. A good load said nothing at all. It only got heavier.

The Ferrous Gate came out of the haze the way it always came, all at once and finished, as though it had been standing a step ahead of him the whole morning. Two iron uprights sunk into the roadbed. A lintel laid across them with nothing above it. No wall on either side, no fence, no ditch, nothing whatsoever to stop a man from walking around the outside of it and carrying on. Men had walked around it. The Road counted that as a debt too, and priced it worse than the toll.

Wren stopped at the white line, eight paces short, and let the frame's foot down onto the stone. His shoulders stayed up where the straps had put them.

The toll board hung on the left upright, and the System kept it current:

**FERROUS GATE — POSTED TOLL**
**Passage, laden: 7 days**
**Sealed cargo: subject to inspection**

Seven. He had walked the whole of that stretch on seven, had spent it in advance the way you do, and here it was, posted and agreeing with him. He worked his thumb up under the strap where it had cut a line into the meat above his collarbone, and he kept his eyes on the numbers while he did it. Sometimes they moved while you watched them.

The collector's window was a slot in the right upright at elbow height, and the ledger came through it before Haro did. A great splayed book with a spine like a wagon axle, laid open and flat on the sill. Then the man behind it. Long grey coat, gate-keys on a ring he never seemed to use for anything, and the face of somebody who had been reading columns of figures for most of his life.

"Name."

"You know my name."

"The book doesn't." Haro did not look up. "Name."

"Idren." He said it the way he always said it, carefully, like a word borrowed out of another language. "Wren, on the road."

The pen found the line.

**IDREN — porter, indentured, Ferrous Gate.**

Under it ran a column of small dates going back a year and a little more, each with a number set beside it, and at the foot of the column two figures. He had long since stopped reading down to reach them. His eye went where they were.

**Days owed: 4,027**
**Days paid: 52**

"Laden," Haro said. "Sealed?"

"Sealed."

"Set it down."

Wren backed the frame against the upright and worked the ropes off their hooks, and the crate came away from his spine with that terrible lightness that is not the same thing as relief. Pale wood, banded at the corners. Across the lid a wax seal the colour of a burn that has healed over, stamped with a mark he did not recognise and had not asked anybody about. He had been carrying it since the low bridges. It never sloshed. It never knocked. Whatever was inside it had been fitted to the inside of it exactly.

Haro came out through the gate's small door, walked once around the crate, and laid two fingers flat on the wax without breaking it. He stood that way for a moment, the way a physician stands.

"Seven for the passage," he said. "Two for the seal. Gate's discretion on unopened cargo."

"The board says seven."

"The board says *sealed cargo: subject to inspection.* This is the inspection." Haro lifted his fingers off the wax. "Nine days."

Wren ran the arithmetic he had run a thousand times before and would run a thousand times again, and it came out the way it always came out, which was no. Nine was nine. Nine was a fortnight out of some winter forty years off, an afternoon somewhere that he would now simply not have, and he was spending it here, on cold stone, over a smear of wax.

"Nine," he said.

"Consent aloud. You know the form."

"I consent to the toll of nine days against passage of the Ferrous Gate, laden and sealed."

The System took them.

It was not pain. He had told a man that once and the man had not believed him, and after that Wren had stopped trying to explain it. It was subtraction. Something in the meat of him that had been counting quietly since the day he was born stepped back nine, and his knees understood it before the rest of him did, and the cold coming up out of the stone through his boots found less to push against than it had found a minute earlier. He breathed out. The haze on the far side of the gate looked exactly as it had looked before.

**TOLL PAID — 9 days**
**FERROUS GATE — passage granted, laden, sealed**

Haro was already writing. Three motions of the pen, no more, and Wren watched the two figures at the bottom of his column get struck through and written again beneath.

**Days owed: 4,018**
**Days paid: 61**

Then the receipt. A chit of grey card with the day's mark pressed into it wet, pushed across the sill with one finger.

Wren took it. He brought out his own book, a cheap sewn thing whose first four pages were still swollen from a river, and he wrote the date, and *Ferrous, laden+seal, 9*, and under that the running total in his own hand, because a man who does not keep his own count is only borrowing somebody else's.

He was writing the 61 when he looked further up the page.

Above his line stood the last porter's. A woman's name he did not know. Four entries. And at the foot of them a paid-total that did not match what those four entries came to. Not by much. By one.

"Something," Haro said.

"No." Wren blew on the ink. "Nothing."

He got the frame back onto his shoulders and took the crate's weight onto a spine nine days shorter, and walked under the lintel, and the iron did not touch him.
